narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 74.7% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process uses this prediction to assess risk, your application was rejected.

The three factors that mattered most were your class rank in your third year of law school, your LSAT score, and your first-year class rank. Your third-year ranking had the strongest influence and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. Being in the second decile is well below the average of roughly sixth decile among students who were accepted, signaling that your later academic performance was weaker than most successful applicants. This was the main reason the model saw high risk.

Your LSAT score was the second most important factor and worked in the opposite direction. At 38, you actually scored slightly above the average of accepted students (37.18), which helped pull the prediction toward passing. Unfortunately, this positive signal was not strong enough to overcome the academic ranking concerns.

Your first-year ranking came third in importance and again pushed toward failure. Placing in the third decile is noticeably lower than the sixth-decile average of accepted students, reinforcing the pattern of below-average performance in law school.

Taken together, the model concluded that your academic record in law school raised too high a risk of bar exam failure. To improve your chances next time, focus on strengthening your academic record if you retake courses, consider additional bar-preparation support, or explore schools that weigh different factors more heavily. Many applicants improve their outcomes by addressing exactly these performance gaps. (248 words)
